Co. for Regional European Air Transport''' ({{langx|de|Crossair AG für europäischen Regionalluftverkehr}}) was a [[Switzerland|Swiss]] [[regional airline]] headquartered on the grounds of [[EuroAirport Basel Mulhouse Freiburg]] in [[Saint-Louis, Haut-Rhin]], [[France]], near [[Basel]], Switzerland. After taking over most of the assets of [[Swissair]] following that airline's bankruptcy in 2002, Crossair was restructured to become [[SWISS]].[https://www.ch-aviation.com/portal/airline/LX ch-aviation.com - Swiss] retrieved 11 March 2023 ==History== Moritz Suter founded the airline in February 1975 as a private company under the name Business Flyers Basel AG.{{Cite web |title=Der Spirit war sagenhaft|url=https://www.volksstimme.ch/der-spirit-war-sagenhaft|website=volksstimme.ch|language=de}} The company operated under this initial name for several years before undergoing a significant change on November 18, 1978, the name was officially changed to Crossair. Scheduled services began shortly thereafter, on July 2, 1979, with flights connecting [[Zürich]] to [[Nuremberg]], [[Innsbruck]], and [[Klagenfurt]].{{Cite web |title=Entrepreneur’s charter airline goes bust|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/demographics/entrepreneur-s-charter-airline-goes-bust/33779212|website=swissinfo.ch}} As the new decade began, Crossair committed to fleet expansion, placing an order in 1980 for ten [[Saab 340]] aircraft.{{Cite web |title=Saab 340 Super Trouper|url=https://www.key.aero/article/saab-340-super-trouper|website=key.aero}} The first of these, registered HB-AHA, was delivered on June 6, 1984, and entered service soon after on June 15, flying between Basel and [[Paris Charles de Gaulle]]. Notably, [[Pope John Paul II]] was one of the dignitaries on this inaugural flight.{{Cite web |title=6/15/1984: Saab 340 Enters Service with Crossair|url=https://www.airwaysmag.com/new-post/saab-340-enters-service-crossair|website=airwaysmag.com}} In 1994, Crossair continued its partnership with [[Saab AB|Saab]] by becoming a launch customer for the [[Saab 2000]], a high-speed turboprop the airline affectionately nicknamed "Concordio." This was a pivotal aircraft for the company, which would ultimately operate 34 of them before its closure, taking delivery of the final manufactured Saab 2000 in 1999.{{cite web|url=https://www.airwaysmag.com/new-post/maiden-flight-saab-2000|author=Lee Cross|title=3/26/1992: MAIDEN FLIGHT OF THE SAAB 2000|publisher=Airways Publishing LLC|date=2024-03-26|accessdate=2024-09-06|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240906052831/https://www.airwaysmag.com/new-post/maiden-flight-saab-2000|archive-date=2024-09-06|url-status=live}}{{Cite web |title=Crossair takes last Saab 2000|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/crossair-takes-last-saab-2000/26158.article|website=flightglobal.com}} The Saab 2000 fleet also supported Crossair's cargo partnership operations with [[DHL]] and [[FedEx]].{{Cite web |title=Crossair President Moritz Suter finds the Saab 2000 is perfect for DHL, UPS and Federal Express|url=https://aviationweek.com/crossair-president-moritz-suter-finds-saab-2000-perfect-dhl-ups-federal-express|website=aviationweek.com/}} In 1992, Crossair were a founder member of the [[Qualiflyer]] frequent flyer scheme alongside Swissair and [[Austrian Airlines]].{{cite book |last=Das |first=T.K. |title=Managing Alliance Portfolios and Networks |publisher=IAP |page= 96|isbn=168123906X }} A change in ownership structure occurred in 1995. [[Swissair]], Crossair's then-parent company, acquired a two-thirds majority stake in the airline as part of the financing agreement for Crossair's purchase of 12 Avro [[RJ100]] jets, with a further 12 options..{{Cite web |title=Crossair seeks cash for RJ100s|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/crossair-seeks-cash-for-rj100s/12669.article|website=flightglobal.com}}{{cite journal |date=1 April 1995 |title=Contracts |url=https://www.emerald.com/aeat/article-abstract/67/4/43/47639/Contracts |journal=Aircraft Engineering |volume=67 |issue=4 |publisher=Emerald |pages=43-44 |access-date=15 December 2025}} At this time, Swissair outsourced its regional flight operations to Crossair, alongside absorbing loss-making charter flights of Balair which had recently merged with Compagnie de Transport Aérien.{{cite journal |date=1995 |title=Flight and the Aircraft Engineer |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Flight_and_the_Aircraft_Engineer/RUSrOkxZ-zIC?hl=en&gbpv=0&bsq=%22Crossair%22%20-wikipedia |journal=Flight and the Aircraft Engineer|volume=147 |publisher=IPC Transport Press Limited |pages=16 |access-date=4 January 2026}} [[File:Crossair Saab 2000 Manteufel-1.jpg|thumb|The Phantom of the Opera livery in July 1995]] Throughout the mid-1990s, Crossair distinguished itself through creative marketing, including unique aircraft liveries. In 1995, the airline teamed up with [[Andrew Lloyd Webber]] and [[The Phantom of the Opera (1986 musical)|The Phantom of the Opera]] to create a unique livery celebrating the musical's opening in Basel.{{Cite web |title=Phantom of the skies|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/phantom-of-the-skies/15468.article|website=flightglobal.com}} Crossair also worked with [[McDonald's]] to create the famous "McPlane," a distinctively red aircraft featuring the iconic logos that even served McDonald's food onboard.{{Cite web |title=Flying the McDonald's McPlane|url=https://www.airwaysmag.com/legacy-posts/mcdonalds-mcplane|website=airwaysmag.com}} As the airline progressed into 1998, they launched [[Crossair Europe]], operating flights from the French side of [[EuroAirport]] to circumvent challenges of European Union restrictions on Swiss air traffic and routes.{{Cite web |title=CROSSAIR EUROPE DEBUT|url=https://aviationweek.com/crossair-europe-debut|website=aviationweek.com}}{{Cite web |title=Crossair bases new sister in France|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/crossair-bases-new-sister-in-france/18997.article|website=flightglobal.com}} Seeking further fleet modernization, Crossair assessed an order to become a launch customer for the new [[Fairchild Dornier 728 family|Fairchild Dornier 728JET]]. However, the airline later decided against this purchase, instead canceling the orders and opting to buy Embraer's new [[Embraer_E-Jet_family#E-170_and_175|ERJ170]] jet.{{Cite web |title=The tale of the 728JET: Fairchild Dornier’s big bet|url=https://www.key.aero/article/tale-728jet-fairchild-dorniers-big-bet|website=key.aero}} [[Embraer]] later explored the development of a shortened version of the E170 specifically tailored for Crossair's needs.{{Cite web |title=Embraer studies short-field ERJ-170 for Crossair|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/embraer-studies-short-field-erj-170-for-crossair/29766.article|website=flightglobal.com}} In 2000, Crossair suffered their first major accident when [[Crossair Flight 498|Flight 498]] crashed minutes after takeoff from Zurich airport.{{Cite web |title=Final Report|url=https://www.sust.admin.ch/inhalte/AV-berichte/1781_e.pdf|website=admin.ch}} The crash came in the midst of a bitter labor-management dispute between Crossair and its pilots over a possible pay raise and work rules changes. The pilots' union had just canceled pay agreements with Crossair in December 1999, with a termination effective in summer 2000. In addition, and prior to the accident, two Crossair pilots told Swiss media that some foreign pilots employed by Crossair posed a safety risk because of an insufficient knowledge of English. These two pilots were fired by Crossair, but were then elected to head the pilots' union, "Crossair Cockpit Personnel (CCP)".{{Cite news|last=Abegg|first=Ernst E.|date=11 January 2000|title=Plane went into dive, turned right before crashing, investigators say|work=AP NEWS|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|url=|access-date=}}[http://www.aviationnow.com/avnow/news/channel_businessweekly.jsp Weekly of Business Aviation.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080820055831/http://www.aviationnow.com/avnow/news/channel_businessweekly.jsp |date=20 August 2008 }} (17 January 2000). ''First Crossair Fatal Crash Comes Amid Labor, Management Turmoil.'' Volume 70; issue 3; p. 27. An investigation of the accident later revealed that the pilot of Flight 498 Pavel Gruzin and copilot Rastislav Kolesár were only able to communicate with each other in English, but Gruzin's ability to speak English was too limited to hold more than a basic conversation.Abegg, Ernst E. (23 August 2002). [[Associated Press]]. ''Investigators: Pilot in fatal Swiss crash was taking tranquilizers.'' In October 2000, a Crossair aircraft at [[Luxembourg Airport]] was attacked by two men armed with [[Kalashnikov rifle|Kalashnikov]] assault rifles in an attempted robbery of bank notes being loaded onto the plane. The pilot was completing an external safety inspection of the aircraft at the time, with no passengers onboard the aircraft. Police were involved in an exchange of gunfire leaving six people injured.{{Cite web |title=Six injured in attack on Crossair plane|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/demographics/six-injured-in-attack-on-crossair-plane/1696262|website=swissinfo.ch}}{{Cite web |title=Crossair Pilot in Ramp Shootout|url=https://aviationweek.com/crossair-pilot-ramp-shootout|website=aviationweek.com}}{{Cite web |title=In Europe, Airport Heists Reveal a Big Security Gap|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB1036706288458074948|website=wsj.com}} The incidents coincided with the airlines first significant financial loss since 1992, of $3.5 million.{{Cite web |title=Crossair lands in the red|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/crossair-lands-in-the-red/1625076|website=swissinfo.ch}} By 2001, Swissair's stake in the regional airline had increased to 70%. However, this year also marked the start of the final chapter for both companies. After parent company [[SAirGroup]] filed for a debt restructuring moratorium in October 2001, an overhaul of the entire operation became unavoidable.{{Cite web |title=A nation in shock: Swissair crisis|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/programmes/crossing_continents/1677085.stm|website=bbc.co.uk}} Suter, remaining as CEO, called the alliance with Swissair through [[Qualiflyer]] into question suggesting his airline may break-away from the group.{{Cite web |title=Swissair confirms commitment to Qualiflyer group|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/swissair-confirms-commitment-to-qualiflyer-group/2086606|website=swissinfo.ch}} A month later, a second fatal crash for Crossair occurred when [[Crossair Flight 3597|Flight 3597]] crashed in a wooded area near [[Bassersdorf]] whilst on final approach to Zurich airport. The Swiss [[Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (Switzerland)|Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau]] (AAIB). The AAIB would conclude that the accident was a [[controlled flight into terrain]] (CFIT) caused by a series of [[pilot error]]s and [[air navigation|navigation]] mistakes that led the plane off-course.{{Cite web |title=Schlussbericht Nr. 1793 des Büros für Flugunfalluntersuchungen über den Unfall des Flugzeuges AVRO 146-RJ100, HB-IXM, betrieben durch Crossair unter Flugnummer CRX 3597, vom 24. November 2001 bei Bassersdorf/ZH |url=https://www.sust.admin.ch/inhalte/AV-berichte/1793_d.pdf |access-date=June 24, 2025 |publisher=Swiss Aircraft accident investigation bureau |pages=12, 130 |language=de |format=PDF}} Of the 33 occupants, 9 survived including Swiss politician [[Jacqueline Badran]].{{Citation|title=Schweiz aktuell - Crossair-Absturz vor 10 Jahren bei Bassersdorf - Play SRF|url=https://www.srf.ch/play/tv/schweiz-aktuell/video/crossair-absturz-vor-10-jahren-bei-bassersdorf?urn=urn:srf:video:b74c3c3e-a4e7-4fea-b12c-049a4df1fb2a|language=de|access-date=2021-02-02}} Among the 24 people that lost their lives in the accident were [[Melanie Thornton]], the former lead singer of the German Eurodance duo [[La Bouche]], and singers [[Passion Fruit (group)#Second-generation line-up|Nathaly van het Ende]] and [[Passion Fruit (group)#Second-generation line-up|Maria Serrano Serrano]] of the German-Dutch Eurodance trio [[Passion Fruit (group)|Passion Fruit]]; the group's third singer, [[Passion Fruit (group)#Second-generation line-up|Debby St. Maarten]] did survive the accident, albeit with significant injuries.{{cite news|url=http://www.nzz.ch/2001/11/27/zh/article7tcs2_1.503442.html|title=Liste der tödlich Verunglückten|date=27 November 2001|newspaper=[[Neue Zürcher Zeitung]]|accessdate=11 December 2009|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130115203007/http://www.nzz.ch/2001/11/27/zh/article7tcs2_1.503442.html|archive-date=15 January 2013|url-status=dead|language=German|trans-title=List of fatally injured}}{{Cite web |title=US singer feared dead in Swiss crash|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/entertainment/1675542.stm|website=bbc.co.uk}} The head of Crossair at the time, André Dosé, confirmed the families of those affected would receive compensation of 30,000 [[Swiss franc|CHF]]. Several years later, seven executives of the former airline were charged for their actions concerning the Flight 3597.{{Cite web |title= Managers charged over fatal Crossair crash|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/demographics/managers-charged-over-fatal-crossair-crash/6215422|website=swissinfo.ch}} After legal proceedings, the defendants were acquitted in 2008.{{Cite web |title=Court acquits former Crossair managers over RJ100 crash|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/court-acquits-former-crossair-managers-over-rj100-crash/80341.article|website=flightglobal.com}} The Swiss federal prosecutor did not appeal the decision. André Dosé and Moritz Suter were awarded a combined compensation settlement of 200,000 CHF whilst four managers were awarded 100,000 CHF each.{{Cite web |title= No appeal in case of doomed Crossair flight|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/demographics/no-appeal-in-case-of-doomed-crossair-flight/7176442|website=swissinfo.ch}}{{cite book |last=Michaelides-Mateou |first=Sofia |date=15 April 2016 |title=Flying in the Face of Criminalization |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Flying_in_the_Face_of_Criminalization/GfgFDAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0 |location=United Kingdom |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9781317134671 |access-date=4 January 2026}} During the ensuing chaos of late 2001, Crossair was pulled into a legal battle with [[Air Liberté]], a former Swissair-owned subsidiary.{{Cite web |title=Crossair's Entire Board Quits, And the Founder Steps Down|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/12/07/business/crossair-s-entire-board-quits-and-the-founder-steps-down.html|website=nytimes.com}} This dispute resulted in the impounding of a Crossair [[Embraer 145]] aircraft in [[Nice]], though Crossair denied liability for Swissair’s debts.{{Cite web |title=French airline files lawsuits against Crossair|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/french-airline-files-lawsuits-against-crossair/2412026|website=swissinfo.ch}}{{Cite web |title=Impounded Crossair jet returns to Switzerland|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/impounded-crossair-jet-returns-to-switzerland/2434284|website=swissinfo.ch}} Despite these legal and financial hurdles, Crossair became the vehicle for the "Phoenix" plan to revive a national Swiss airline, with the Canton of Zurich voting to inject 300million CHF into the new project.{{Cite web |title= Sunday vote to determine airline “Phoenix” plan|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/sunday-vote-to-determine-airline-phoenix-plan/2475666|website=swissinfo.ch}}{{Cite web |title= Canton Zurich backs crucial Crossair credit plan|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/canton-zurich-backs-crucial-crossair-credit-plan/2480428|website=swissinfo.ch}} On March 31, 2002, Swissair ceased all operations. Crossair subsequently absorbed most of Swissair's assets, underwent a comprehensive restructuring, and was officially rebranded to become Swiss International Air Lines.{{Cite web |title=PR flurry heralds Swissair relaunch|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/1898877.stm|website=bbc.co.uk}}{{Cite web |title=New airline is just plain “swiss”|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/new-airline-is-just-plain-swiss/2516586|website=swissinfo.ch}} ==Head office== In the early 1980s, Crossair was based at [[Zurich Airport]] in [[Kloten]]."World Airline Directory." ''Flight International''. 30 March 1985. [http://www.flightglobal.com/pdfarchive/view/1985/1985%20-%200931.html 71]." Retrieved on 17 June 2009. However, as the organisation grew it opened a training centre at [[EuroAirport Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg]] in 1983, before undertaking construction of a new head office at the airport in 1989. This would become the airlines headquarters until 2002, when it became the head office for Swiss International Airlines."[https://web.archive.org/web/20020202015152/http://www.crossair.com/en/ourcompany/location/index.html Location]." Crossair. Retrieved on 13 June 2009."[https://web.archive.org/web/20121102215146/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-88189391.html INDUSTRY BRIEFS.]" ''Airline Industry Information''. 2 July 2002. Retrieved on 12 January 2010. "According to a company statement, the new name replaces Crossair at the corporate headquarters in Basel." ==Destinations== Crossair designed its entire route network around a sophisticated multi-hub business plan, operating primarily from bases in Basel, Bern, Geneva, Lugano, and Zürich. The airline was intensely focused on serving smaller regional airports and efficiently connecting that traffic to larger international airports. This strategy began at the launch of scheduled service on July 2, 1979, with flights immediately connecting Zürich to the German and Austrian cities of [[Nuremberg]], [[Innsbruck]], and [[Klagenfurt]]. The domestic network was crucial, with the airline also maintaining essential internal links, such as flights between [[Lugano]] and Geneva via Basel.{{Cite web |title=Rapport Final du Bureau d’enquête sur les accidents d‘aviation|url=https://www.sust.admin.ch/inhalte/AV-berichte/1723.pdf|website=sust.admin.ch|language=fr}} A core component of this strategy was the innovative Eurocross scheme operating from the Basel base. This system was set up to serve smaller airports and ensure passengers could transfer quickly, with short transfer times, onto onward flights with partner airlines from larger hubs like Zürich.{{Cite web |title=Euro Airport as Regional Hub|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/library/travel/practical/pt990110.html|website=nytimes.com}} As the network matured, specific routes grew, including the 1984 service linking Basel to Paris Charles de Gaulle. Later in the airline’s history, new flights were added to [[Nice]], [[Gothenburg]], [[Manchester]] and [[Leipzig]].{{Cite web |title=More Route Expansion For Crossair|url=https://aviationweek.com/more-route-expansion-crossair|website=aviationweek.com}}{{Cite web |title=Crossair honoured for its noise protection activities|url=https://www.emerald.com/aeat/article/doi/10.1108/aeat.2002.12774aab.023/26674/Crossair-honoured-for-its-noise-protection|website=emerald.com}} Crossair also utilised an [[MD-11]] aircraft in the summer of 1997 to service weekly flights to Palma de Mallorca.{{Cite web |title=Commercial Airlines and the MD11|url=https://jetbackintime.com/2023/01/18/commercial-airlines-and-the-md-11/|website=jetbackintime.com}} To significantly extend its reach across Europe, Crossair cultivated strategic partnerships and feeder agreements. On a regional level, the airline maintained alliances with carriers such as [[Air Europe]], [[Air Littoral]], and [[Tyrolean Airways]]. Crucially, Crossair developed extensive [[codeshare]] and interlining agreements with major flag carriers, integrating its regional network into their global operations. These key partners included [[Austrian Airlines]], [[Air France]], [[British Airways]] and [[TAP Air Portugal]], solidifying Crossair's role as a high-quality feeder airline for global traffic.{{cite book |last=Lawton |first=Thomas C |date=2 March 2017 |title=Cleared for Take-off |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Cleared_for_Take_Off/a0gaEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0 |location=United Kingdom |publisher=Taylor & Francis |page=48-49 |isbn=9781351951029 |access-date=14 December 2025}} The relationship with Swissair also yielded a number of Crossair operated flights beyond Europe, such as the transatlantic Basel to [[Newark Liberty International Airport|Newark]] flight.{{Cite web |title=Moritz Suter - Crossair|url=https://www.bilanz.ch/panorama/moritz-suter-crossair|website=bilanz.ch|language=DE}} ==Fleet== [[File:78at - Crossair Avro RJ 85; HB-IXG@ZRH;30.11.1999 (5257318064).jpg|thumb|Crossair [[Avro RJ85]]]] [[File:Crossair MD-82; HB-INV@ZRH;08.02.1997 (6169435636).jpg|thumb|Crossair [[McDonnell Douglas MD-82]]]] [[File:Crossair Saab 2000; HB-IZG@ZRH;08.02.1997 (6169448356).jpg|thumb|Crossair [[Saab 2000]]]] Crossair has operated the following aircraft throughout its existence:{{cn|date=June 2026}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |+ Crossair fleet |- !Aircraft !Total !Introduced !Retired !Notes |- |[[Avro RJ85]] |4 |1993 |2002 |Transferred to [[Swiss International Air Lines]]. |- |[[Avro RJ100]] |16 |1995 |2002 |Transferred to [[Swiss International Air Lines]].

One written off as [[Swiss International Air Lines Flight 850|Flight 850]]. |- |} ==Accidents and incidents== *21 February 1990: The [[Landing gear|undercarriage]] was accidentally retracted on a [[Crossair]] Saab 340A, registration HB-AHA, on the [[Airport ramp|apron]] at [[Zürich Airport]]. No fatalities, aircraft destroyed.{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Accident Saab 340A HB-AHA, Wednesday 21 February 1990 |url=https://aviation-safety.net/asndb/326088 |access-date=2026-06-05 |website=aviation-safety.net}} The captain involved (Hans Ulrich Lutz) was killed in [[Crossair Flight 3597]] in 2001. *10 January 2000: [[Crossair Flight 498]] crashed just after take-off from [[Zürich]]. All 10 people aboard were killed.{{Cite web|last=Ranter|first=Harro|title=ASN Aircraft accident Saab 340B HB-AKK Nassenwil|url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=20000110-0|access-date=20 August 2020|work=[[Aviation Safety Network]]}} *9 October 2000: Crossair flight SR 3879 was involved in an attempted bank note cargo robbery by armed assailants at Luxembourg Airport. There were no passengers onboard the aircraft at the time. *19 December 2000: A Crossair Saab 2000 slid off the runway at Dresden Airport during takeoff due to a burst tire. All 18 passengers and 4 crew survived unharmed.{{Cite web |title= Crossair plane slides off runway in Dresden|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/crossair-plane-slides-off-runway-in-dresden/1805902|website=swissinfo.ch}} *24 November 2001: [[Crossair Flight 3597]] crashed near [[Zürich]], killing 24 of 33 people aboard, including the former [[La Bouche]] lead singer [[Melanie Thornton]] and two of the three members of the German [[Eurodance]] group [[Passion Fruit (band)|Passion Fruit]]. The third member, Debby St. Maarten, sustained serious injuries but survived.{{cite web|url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=20011124-0|title=Accident description|publisher=Aviation Safety Network|access-date=8 September 2010}} *24 December 2001: A Crossair Avro-RJ85 slid off the runway during a snowstorm on arrival at [[Sarajevo Airport]]. All 88 onboard survived unharmed.{{Cite web |title= Crossair jet skids off runway in Sarajevo|url=https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/banking-fintech/crossair-jet-skids-off-runway-in-sarajevo/2451688|website=swissinfo.ch}} ==See also== *[[Crossair Europe]] *[[Swissair]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{commons category inline|Crossair}} *[https://web.archive.org/web/*/http://www.crossair.com Crossair Website - crossair.com] (Archive) *[https://web.archive.org/web/*/http://crossair.ch/ Crossair Website - crossair.ch] (Archive) {{in lang|de}} *[https://web.archive.org/web/*/www.crossair.ch/en/home/index.html Crossair Website - crossair.ch] (Archive) {{Portalbar|Switzerland|Companies|Aviation}} {{Airlines of Switzerland}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Swissair]] [[Category:Swiss companies established in 1975]] [[Category:Swiss companies disestablished in 2002]] [[Category:Defunct airlines of Switzerland]] [[Category:Airlines established in 1975]] [[Category:Airlines disestablished in 2002]] [[Category:Companies based in Basel]]

Crossair Ltd. Co. for Regional European Air Transport (German: Crossair AG für europäischen Regionalluftverkehr) was a Swiss regional airline headquartered on the grounds of EuroAirport Basel Mulhouse Freiburg in Saint-Louis, Haut-Rhin, France, near Basel, Switzerland. 
After taking over most of the assets of Swissair following that airline's bankruptcy in 2002, Crossair was restructured to become SWISS.
